title: Cerebral lesions in hematological malignancies: a case report
case_prompt:
A 62-year-old Caucasian man with a history of follicular non-Hodgkin lymphoma presented in June 2020 with progressive vision loss. He had been treated initially with R-CHOP in 2010 and, after recurrence in 2017, with R-bendamustine followed by rituximab maintenance until February 2020. During maintenance he experienced recurrent urinary tract infections, gingivitis, and herpes zoster reactivation. On examination he was afebrile with normal vital signs and had a right homonymous hemianopia; the remainder of the neurological and general examinations was unremarkable.

Noncontrast head CT revealed an uneven hypodense cortical and subcortical lesion in the left posterior temporal and occipital lobes without enhancement. MRI demonstrated a left parenchymal lesion with two components: a periventricular area of inhomogeneous T1 hypointensity and T2 hyperintensity, and a more uniform white-matter region of T2 and FLAIR hyperintensity with T1 hypointensity. Both components showed restricted diffusion, and there was no gadolinium enhancement. MR spectroscopy showed decreased N-acetyl aspartate, elevated choline, and a double lactate peak. Total-body contrast CT showed no evidence of active lymphoma and only two stable lymph nodes.

Brain biopsy revealed numerous CD68+ macrophages, isolated reactive astrocytes, and mild perivascular T-lymphocyte infiltrates; no neoplastic cells were identified. No microbiological studies were performed on the tissue. The patient was discharged but returned with worsening vision, mental confusion, and psychomotor slowing. Laboratory studies including CBC, CRP, electrolytes, renal and liver function tests were unremarkable. Repeat MRI showed marked enlargement of the left temporal–parietal–occipital and peritrigonal lesion, now crossing the corpus callosum with vasogenic edema and slight mass effect; there remained no contrast enhancement, and DWI again showed restricted diffusion at the lesion edges.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ischemia considered but excluded — “Ischemia can be excluded if the lesion does not conform to any cerebrovascular territory and, above all, if it expands significantly on follow-up imaging.”  
2. CNS lymphoma considered but excluded — “the absence of significant contrast enhancement and, above all, the inconclusive response of previous histological report excluded the hypothesis of an expanding neoplastic lesion.”  
3. Low-grade glioma considered but excluded — “spectroscopy reduction of N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak and choline and lactate peak elevation were less consistent with this hypothesis … moreover, it grew too fast.”  
4. High-grade glioma considered but excluded — “there was no evidence of pathological neovascularization and no necrosis area, hemorrhage, or calcification, and there was no marked mass effect or perilesional edema … no histological confirmation.”  
5. Metastasis considered but excluded — “metastasis was excluded because of no other detectable neoplastic localization on total-body CT, no distinctive imaging features … and no histological feedback.”
